title: What Does What You Own Say About What You’ll Buy Next? A Marketer’s Guide to Ownership Data
summary: Learn how ownership data helps marketers understand consumer needs, improve audience targeting, enrich CRM data, and build more relevant audiences.
body_markdown:
What is ownership data? A house. A car. Maybe two cars.


The things consumers already own can tell marketers something important about what they may need next.


A[homeowner has different needs than a renter](https://porchgroupmedia.com/blog/homeowners-renters-and-property-signals-in-2026/) . Someone driving an older vehicle may have different needs than someone with a newer one. And the characteristics of a home can create entirely different opportunities for products and services.


**What consumers own adds another layer of context to who they are.**


And when ownership data is combined with demographics, household information, lifestyle interests, and in-market behavior, marketers have even more ways to build relevant audiences.


Key takeaways


- Ownership data covers two high-value categories: home and property, and automotive.


- Homeowner versus renter status alone changes the relevance of entire product categories.


- Vehicle detail (VIN, make, model, year) separates a useful automotive audience from a generic “vehicle owner” list.


- Ownership indicates likely need. It does not predict a specific purchase.


- Ownership becomes most useful layered with lifestyle interests and in-market intent signals.


- Ownership data also enriches the customers already in your CRM, not just prospects.


## What Is Ownership Data?


Ownership data is information about the assets, products, and characteristics associated with a consumer or household: whether they own or rent their home, the details of that property, and the vehicles they drive. Marketers use it to understand what is already part of a consumer’s life before deciding what to offer them next.


With[People Factors](https://porchgroupmedia.com/consumer-data/) , that can include insights across two particularly valuable areas:


- [Home and property](https://porchgroupmedia.com/property-owner-data/) **:** Homeownership and detailed property information


- [Automotive](https://porchgroupmedia.com/automotive-data/) **:** Vehicle ownership, VIN, make, model, year, and additional vehicle characteristics


People Factors connects these ownership insights with broader consumer and household information, including demographics, finances, lifestyle and interests, browsing activity, and in-market intent.


That combination can help marketers move beyond simply asking:


**Who fits our target demographic?**


And start asking:


**Who has a reason to need what we sell?**


## Homeowner vs. Renter: How Homeownership Data Changes the Marketing Opportunity


Start with one of the biggest distinctions: homeowner or renter. That single characteristic can immediately change the relevance of entire categories. Homeowners may have needs related to:


- Home improvement


- Repair and maintenance


- Furniture and décor


- Lawn and garden


- Home services


- Insurance


- Home technology


- Appliances


- Financial products


But even “homeowner” is still a very broad audience. The property itself can provide more context.


PGM’s People Factors framework connects[consumer information with property and homeowner insights](https://porchgroupmedia.com/blog/what-is-consumer-data/) , giving marketers the ability to understand people alongside the homes they live in.


Depending on the campaign, that can create opportunities to build audiences around the characteristics that actually matter to what you’re selling.

## What’s in the Driveway: How Vehicle and Automotive Data Works


A vehicle can tell marketers more than whether someone owns a car. PGM’s Auto Factors automotive data set includes:


- VIN


- Make


- Model


- Year


- Engine size


- Fuel type


- Drivetrain


- Engine block


- Engine cylinders


- Additional consumer and financing insights


PGM also uses daily, weekly, and monthly processes to track vehicle dispositions and suppress vehicles that are no longer on the road.


That creates a much more detailed picture of automotive ownership than simply “vehicle owner.”


And depending on the marketer, different pieces of that picture may matter.


- An automotive service company may care about different vehicle characteristics than a dealership.


- An insurance marketer may have different criteria again.


- An automotive accessories company may want something entirely different.


**The value of the data depends on the marketing question you’re trying to answer.**


## What Ownership Data Reveals About Consumer Needs


Ownership data becomes interesting because products often create additional needs.


Own a home? That home needs to be maintained.


Own a vehicle? That vehicle needs service, insurance, parts, and eventually replacement.


Own a particular type of property or vehicle? That can create an entirely different set of potential needs.


This doesn’t mean this data can tell you with certainty what someone will purchase next. But it can help marketers identify consumers for whom a particular product or service is more likely to be relevant.


And that’s an important distinction.


**Good audience building isn’t about predicting every consumer’s next move. It’s about creating more context around who has a reason to care about your offer.**


## Combining Ownership Data With Lifestyle and Interest Data


Ownership tells you one thing. Interests can tell you something else.


Imagine a home improvement marketer. You could start with:


**Homeowners.**


Then identify:


**Homeowners interested in home improvement and DIY.**


Or perhaps a brand sells products specifically for outdoor living.


Now gardening, outdoor activities, property information, and other lifestyle characteristics may become relevant too.


The People Factors consumer data includes hundreds of attributes spanning demographics, lifestyle, purchase behavior, and other consumer characteristics.


The point isn’t to layer data just because it’s available.


It’s to combine the attributes that make sense for the product you’re marketing.


## Layering In-Market Intent Data on Top of Ownership Data


Ownership tells you what someone has. Intent data can add insight into what they may be considering.


That’s where the combination becomes particularly useful.


PGM’s[online intent data](https://porchgroupmedia.com/intent-data/) identifies high-intent consumers based on what they’re browsing, engaging with, and reading online.


For example:


**Ownership:**
Consumer owns a vehicle.


**More context:**
You know the make, model, and year.


**Add intent:**
The consumer is now actively browsing automotive content and may be in-market for another vehicle.


PGM’s automotive data specifically supports identifying in-market car shoppers based on online browsing activity, including consumers likely to purchase a vehicle within the next 90 days.


Or consider a home-related campaign:


**Ownership:**
Consumer owns a home.


**Add lifestyle:**
Consumer has relevant home improvement interests.


**Add intent:**
Consumer is actively browsing products or services related to what you sell.


Each piece adds context.


## Using Ownership Data to Enrich First-Party and CRM Data


This data isn’t only useful for prospecting. It can also add another dimension to the customers already sitting in your CRM.


Your first-party data might tell you:


- What they purchased from you


- When they purchased


- How much they spent


- How frequently they buy


- How they engage with your company


People Factors can add context around:


- Whether they own a home


- The property associated with them


- What vehicle or vehicles they own


- Demographic and household characteristics


- Lifestyle and interests


- Current online browsing and in-market behavior


Now you have more information to explore potential opportunities for segmentation, personalization, cross-sell, upsell, and retention.


## Frequently Asked Questions About Ownership Data


**What is ownership data in marketing?**


Ownership data is information about the assets and characteristics associated with a consumer or household, such as homeownership status, property details, and vehicle ownership. Marketers use it to identify consumers for whom a product or service is more likely to be relevant.


**What is the difference between ownership data and demographic data?**


Demographic data describes who someone is (age, income, household composition). Ownership data describes what is already part of their life. A homeowner and a renter can share identical demographics and still have entirely different needs for home services, insurance, or appliances.


**How is automotive ownership data used for targeting?**


Automotive data can include VIN, make, model, year, engine size, fuel type, and drivetrain. Different marketers use different pieces: a service company, a dealership, an insurance marketer, and an accessories brand each care about different vehicle characteristics.


**Can ownership data predict what a consumer will buy next?**


No. Ownership data cannot tell you with certainty what someone will purchase. It can identify consumers who have a reason to care about a specific offer, which is a more realistic and more useful goal for audience building.


**How does ownership data work with first-party CRM data?**


First-party data tells you what a customer bought from you and how they engage. Ownership data adds outside context: whether they own a home, what property they live in, what vehicles they own, and what they are currently browsing. That combination supports segmentation, cross-sell, upsell, and retention.


## Don’t Just Ask Who They Are. Ask What They Own.


Demographics are useful. Interests are useful. Behavior and intent are useful. But ownership can answer a completely different question:


**What is already part of this consumer’s life?**


A home. A particular property. A vehicle. A particular make, model, and year.


Those details can provide additional context around the products and services that may be relevant to a consumer.


And when you connect ownership with household, demographic, lifestyle, behavioral, and in-market data, you can build audiences around much more than a generic customer profile.


**Sometimes understanding what someone already has can help you better understand what they may need next.**
